t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The aim of this session is to familiarise students with the toxicological significance and the methods of analysis of mineral acids, alkalis and their salts. The plan has two parts: the first is dialysis and the toxicological significance of the poisons that are isolated from the object with water and then detected, the second is the methods of isolating them and detecting them in the dialysate. Within the topic, of the mineral acids, sulphuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids are considered.

Expected outcome: students master the conditions for isolating mineral acids, alkalis and their salts and detecting them in the dialysate. Items needed: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids. As for laboratory equipment, the session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

About safety and preparation. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis and AIDS, arrive in a special container and are noted in the documents.

By dialysis, mainly mineral acids, alkalis and salts that dissolve well in water are isolated. In practice, cases of poisoning occur with sulphuric, nitric and hydrochloric acids, sodium and potassium hydroxides, and an aqueous solution of ammonia. Poisoning also occurs with compounds of nitric and nitrous acids with various alkalis, that is their salts.

Let us consider the poisons isolated by dialysis, dividing them into three groups. Mineral acids: sulphuric acid, nitric acid, hydrochloric acid. Alkalis: sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and an aqueous solution of ammonia. Salts: nitrites, that is NaNO2 and KNO2, and nitrates. All of them are united as water-soluble poisons.

t: Two methods of isolating water-soluble poisons
n: There are two methods of isolating water-soluble poisons. The first method: the minced object is shaken with purified water and the aqueous layer is filtered. The drawback of this method is that, owing to parts of the object dissolving in water, many foreign substances are released and interfere with the analysis. The second method is dialysis, in which a parchment beaker and a crystalliser are used.

t: Two methods of isolation with water: comparison
n: Let us compare the two methods. In shaking and filtering, the minced object is shaken with water from time to time and the aqueous layer is filtered, but many foreign substances are released. In dialysis, a crystalliser of 2-3 l and a long parchment beaker are taken, the liquid level in both vessels is the same, and the water is changed after 4-6 hours. Dialysis therefore lets fewer foreign substances through.

Procedure for carrying out dialysis. Water is poured into a 2-3 litre crystalliser; a long parchment beaker with its bottom cut off is lowered in. A mixture of the object and water is placed in the beaker; the liquid level in both vessels must be the same. After 4-6 hours the water is poured off into another beaker and fresh water is added. At the end the dialysates are combined.

The main figures in dialysis. For dialysis, a crystalliser of 2-3 litres is taken. After 4-6 hours, the water in the crystalliser is poured into another beaker and fresh water is added. The dialysate is evaporated on a water bath until 10-20 ml remains. Remember these three figures: the volume, the time and the evaporation residue.

Preparing the dialysate for analysis. The liquid obtained by filtration or dialysis is evaporated on a water bath until 10-20 ml remains. The residue is examined for the analysis of water-soluble toxic substances. Before detecting a specific substance, the dialysate is checked for the presence of strong mineral acids or alkalis.

Preliminary testing with indicators. Various indicators are added to a portion of the dialysate. Universal indicator paper turns red. Congo red turns blue. Tropaeolin 00 and dimethylaminoazobenzene turn red. Methyl violet turns blue. These changes indicate the presence of strong mineral acids.

Why distil first and then analyse? In the dialysate, chloride, sulphate and nitrate ions cannot be tested directly: they enter the body constantly, and some are formed in metabolism. Therefore the mineral acids are first distilled from the dialysate and then analysed. If free sulphuric acid is present, hydrochloric acid can always be found in the distillate. For this reason the analysis begins with sulphuric acid.

t: Distilling sulphuric acid with copper: scheme
n: Scheme of distilling sulphuric acid with copper. Copper powder is added to the dialysate and it is distilled in a distillation apparatus. Sulphuric acid reacts with copper and is converted into the readily distilled sulphur dioxide, SO2. The dioxide reacts with iodine in the receiving flask and again forms the sulphate anion. SO4 is determined in the decolourised distillate.

t: Sulphuric acid: signs of poisoning and distillation
n: In poisoning with sulphuric acid, the tissues of the lips, tongue and stomach of the person who drank it are damaged; the acid ruins clothing. Copper powder is added to the dialysate and it is distilled; the receiving flask contains a solution of iodine in KI. Sulphur dioxide reacts with iodine and again gives the sulphate anion. At the end the excess iodine is removed.

Steps of detecting sulphuric acid. The distillate is heated until the excess iodine has gone; the sulphate ion is determined in the colourless liquid. When 1-2 drops of 5% barium chloride are added to 3-5 drops of distillate, a white precipitate forms. If 2-3 drops of a 3% solution of lead acetate are added, a white precipitate also forms. The red spot formed with sodium rhodizonate fades under the action of sulphuric acid.

t: Reactions for the sulphate ion: Ba and Pb
n: Reactions for the sulphate ion. The reactions are carried out in the decolourised distillate, that is one from which the excess iodine has been removed. If 1-2 drops of 5% BaCl2 are added to 3-5 drops, a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in HNO3, HCl or alkali. If 3% lead acetate is added to a few drops, a white precipitate also forms; it does not dissolve in HNO3 and dissolves in alkali. Both reactions form a white precipitate; they differ in the solubility of the precipitate.

Reaction with sodium rhodizonate. 1-2 drops of 1% BaCl2 are applied to paper, then a drop of fresh 0.2% sodium rhodizonate: a red spot forms. If 1-2 drops of distillate are applied to this spot, the red colour disappears when sulphuric acid is present. This reaction is considered characteristic in detecting sulphuric acid.

In poisoning with nitric acid, the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract and, in some cases, the skin of the face may turn yellowish. If the poisoning was with an acid weaker than a 20% solution, yellow colouring of the skin may not be observed. Nitric acid is distilled from the dialysate, as is sulphuric acid, in the presence of copper powder.

t: Distilling nitric acid with copper: scheme
n: Scheme of distilling nitric acid with copper. Nitric acid is distilled from the dialysate in a distillation apparatus in the presence of copper powder, as with sulphuric acid. In the reaction, NO forms first, then NO2. As a result, nitric and nitrous acids, HNO3 and HNO2, form in the receiving flask.

Reactions for the nitrate ion. The nitric and nitrous acids formed in the receiving flask are determined by the following reactions. 1% diphenylamine in H2SO4 gives a bluish colour with the distillate. If 2-3 drops of 0.02% brucine are added to the distillate, a red colour forms. Remember: both reactions are also given by nitrites and other oxidising agents.

Let us compare the diphenylamine and brucine reactions. Diphenylamine: if a drop of distillate is added to 4-5 drops of a 1% solution, a bluish colour forms. Brucine: if a freshly prepared 0.02% solution is added, a red colour appears when nitric acid is present. Both reactions are also given by nitrites and other oxidising agents, so their result is not a final confirmation.

t: Wool and cotton test and removing nitrites
n: The wool and cotton test. Nitric acid forms a stable yellow compound with the protein of wool; if washed with water, the colour of the wool does not fade. A material woven from cotton, however, loses its yellow colour. Because diphenylamine and brucine are positive in the presence of nitrite as well, nitrites are determined first, for which sulphanilic acid or Griess reagent is used.

Sequence of nitrate analysis. Before analysing for nitric acid, it is necessary to determine the nitrites. The distillate is brought to a neutral medium and tested with sulphanilic acid or Griess reagent. The formation of an azo dye confirms the presence of nitrous acid. After that, the nitrites are removed and the diphenylamine, brucine and wool tests are carried out.

The distillation behaviour of hydrochloric acid. Free hydrochloric acid occurs in small amounts in gastric juice, and its salts in the tissues of the body. The dialysate is distilled without copper powder to a dry residue: the free acid distils over, its salts do not. Water distils first; when the concentration of the solution reaches about 10%, hydrochloric acid begins to distil.

Stages of distilling hydrochloric acid. The dialysate is distilled as in the case of sulphuric acid, but without copper powder. In the first stage, water distils. When the concentration of the solution reaches about 10%, hydrochloric acid begins to distil. Distillation is continued to a dry residue. Free hydrochloric acid distils over, while its salts do not.

Reactions for the chloride ion are carried out in the liquid from the receiving flask. If 1-2 drops of AgNO3 are added to 1-2 ml of the liquid, a white precipitate forms that dissolves in ammonia. If 1-2 ml of the liquid is mixed with crystals of Berthollet's salt, free chlorine gas is released. These two results confirm the chloride ion.

t: Chloride ion: silver nitrate reaction scheme
n: The chloride ion and the silver nitrate reaction. If 1-2 drops of silver nitrate are added to 1-2 ml of distillate, a white precipitate forms; the precipitate dissolves in ammonia solution. When mixed with crystals of Berthollet's salt, free chlorine gas is released. The scheme shows the reagents, the product and the observed sign in this order.

The Carousel training is held on acids. Reagents: barium chloride, silver nitrate, Berthollet's salt, diphenylamine, lead acetate, universal indicators. The table columns: sulphuric, nitric and hydrochloric acids; for each acid, the reagents with which it is detected are shown. Task: to determine which reagent matches which acid, and to write the chemical equation.

Detecting the potassium cation. 1-2 drops of dialysate on a microscope slide are acidified with 1 drop of 6% acetic acid; crystals of sodium nitrite and cobalt nitrate are added. After 15-20 minutes, yellow star-shaped crystals of potassium hexanitrocobaltate are seen under the microscope. In addition: if tartaric acid solution is added to 1-2 ml of dialysate in the cold, a white precipitate forms.

The potassium cation and the hexanitrocobaltate reaction. 1-2 drops of dialysate are acidified on a microscope slide with 6% acetic acid. Crystals of sodium nitrite and cobalt nitrate are added; after 15-20 minutes it is examined under the microscope. Yellow star-shaped crystals of potassium hexanitrocobaltate are seen.

Detecting the sodium cation. 1-2 drops of dialysate are acidified with 1 M acetic acid. Then, if 1 ml of zinc uranyl acetate is added, a yellow precipitate forms. If potassium hydroantimonate is added under cooled conditions, a white precipitate comes out. These are reactions characteristic of the sodium cation.

Let us compare the potassium and sodium cations. For potassium, the hexanitrocobaltate reaction gives yellow stars, while tartaric acid forms a white precipitate in the cold. For sodium, zinc uranyl acetate gives a yellow precipitate, while potassium hydroantimonate gives a white precipitate. For potassium, a solution of tartaric acid in the cold is used; for sodium, acidification with 1 M acetic acid.

Detecting ammonia by the paper strips method. The liquid is placed in a flask, which is closed with a stopper bearing strips of red litmus paper, lead acetate paper and copper sulphate paper. The flask is kept for 1-2 hours, then the strips are examined one after another. With ammonia, the red litmus and copper sulphate papers turn blue, and the lead acetate paper does not change. In putrefaction, the copper sulphate and lead acetate papers turn black. Ammonia can also be determined in the presence of sodium or potassium hydroxide: NH4Cl + NaOH = NH4OH + NaCl.

t: Ammonia and putrefactive sulphide: paper strips result
n: Let us distinguish the result of the paper strips method for ammonia and putrefactive sulphide. The litmus and copper sulphate papers turning blue and the lead acetate paper not changing indicate the presence of ammonia. If the litmus does not change and the copper and lead papers turn black, this indicates the presence of sulphide formed as a result of putrefaction. After the flask has been kept for 1-2 hours, the strips are examined one after another.

Properties of nitrites and preparation. Sodium and potassium nitrites are crystalline substances that dissolve very well in water; they rapidly take up water vapour from the air. Because sodium and potassium salts are always present in the body, in forensic chemical practice it is not stated to which cation the nitrite belongs. The dialysate is brought to neutral conditions, and then the analysis of nitrites and nitrates is carried out.

Reactions for the nitrite ion. The first reaction is carried out in the neutralised dialysate: 0.5% sulphanilic acid and β-naphthol give a reddish colour, that is an azo dye. After waiting 3-5 minutes, an alkaline solution of β-naphthol is added; if there is a lot of nitrite, the azo dye may also precipitate. In the second reaction, if dilute H2SO4 and pure KI are added to 2 ml of dialysate, a brown colour appears, and with starch a light blue. For nitrates, diphenylamine in H2SO4 is used, but nitrites also give this result.

Scheme of the nitrite and sulphanilic acid reaction. To 1-2 ml of neutralised dialysate, 1-2 ml of 0.5% sulphanilic acid in 2% HCl is added. After 3-5 minutes, an alkaline solution of β-naphthol is added. If nitrite is present, a reddish colour forms; if there is a lot, the azo dye may precipitate.

The Carousel training on alkalis and salts. Training columns: NaNO2, KNO2, NH4OH, K+, Na+; reagents: azo dye, zinc uranyl acetate, Na/Co nitrite, diphenylamine, tartaric acid, indicators. Case 25: the isolate obtained from the forensic chemical analysis showed an alkaline medium; carry out the analysis taking into account the ammonia formed in the putrefaction of a corpse. Case table: type of problem, causes of origin and ways of resolving it.

Interpreting the result. A change in the indicators shows only the presence of a strong mineral acid; which acid it is, is determined by reactions in the distillate. The analysis begins with sulphuric acid, because hydrochloric acid may be found in the distillate. The nitrate reactions, that is with diphenylamine and brucine, are positive also with nitrite and other oxidising agents, so nitrite is determined beforehand. In the paper strips method, litmus not changing while the copper and lead papers turn black indicates the presence of sulphide formed by putrefaction.

Review questions. First: which substances are isolated by the dialysis method, on what physical property is the method based, and with what apparatus is it carried out? Second: what is the essence of testing with Congo red, tropaeolin 00 and other indicators; why, in detecting sulphuric acid, is the dialysate distilled with the addition of copper? Third: on what chemical principles are the qualitative and quantitative determination of nitric acid based; why is sulphuric acid analysed before hydrochloric acid? Fourth: when the dialysate is alkaline, how can one determine whether carbonate salts or free alkali are present; why are sodium and potassium hydroxides analysed first?

Conclusion. Dialysis is a method of separating water-soluble acids, alkalis and salts from foreign substances; the dialysate is evaporated to 10-20 ml. Acids are determined in the distillate: sulphuric with BaCl2, lead acetate and rhodizonate, nitric with diphenylamine and brucine, hydrochloric with AgNO3 and Berthollet's salt. Cations and ammonia: K+ is determined with hexanitrocobaltate and tartaric acid, Na+ with zinc uranyl acetate, NH3 with three kinds of paper strips, and nitrites with an azo dye and KI.
